item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO – Pete Crow-Armstrong has piled up the historic feats and footnotes throughout this season, compiling the type of campaign that Cubs manager Craig Counsell said fans will be telling their grandkids about someday. The star center fielder has added yet another exclusive club to the growing list.
On Thursday afternoon, Crow-Armstrong stole second base in the first inning against the Marlins at Wrigley Field to officially enter the 40-40 Club. He is only the seventh player in Major League history to have at least 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases in a single tour, and is the first in Cubs history to do so.
“Everything Pete has done this year has been really incredible,” Counsell said. “I know that’s a milestone, but I think we’ve seen it all already this year, actually, you know? And I think the people here have celebrated him in a really cool way. I’ve never seen it before, actually.”
Counsell noted how Cubs fans have been chanting Crow-Armstrong’s initials since he broke into the big leagues.
During his debut game at Coors Field in Denver in 2023, the “P-C-A” chants also made their MLB debut. It has happened in road cities throughout the big leagues over the past few years, gaining volume as his star power has climbed. They were there in the Tokyo Dome in Japan for the opening series last year. And they are a constant at Wrigley Field during his at-bats or after steals or dynamic plays in center.
This season, they have evolved throughout the summer, becoming cries of “M-V-P” as Crow-Armstrong has blossomed into the game’s best all-around player this year.
“I haven’t seen somebody’s name chanted since he’s been in the league, really,” Counsell said. “It’s really something to perform with all that on a regular basis.”
In the process, Crow-Armstrong’s performance has vaulted him into some elite company.
He joined Shohei Ohtani (54 homers and 59 steals in 2024), Ronald Acuña Jr. (41 homers and 73 steals in ‘23), Alfonso Soriano (46 homers and 41 steals in ‘06), Alex Rodriguez (42 homers and 46 steals in 1998), Barry Bonds (42 homers and 40 steals in ‘96), and Jose Canseco (42 homers and 40 steals in ‘88) as the only players to have a 40-40 season in MLB history.
“I think it’s super cool,” Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said. “There are only so many guys in the game that can even think about accomplishing it. [He’s only] the seventh person ever to do it. The list is pretty amazing, so I think it is neat.”
Crow-Armstrong was already the first player in Cubs history to have at least 40 homers and 30 steals. The center fielder is only the second player – along with Sammy Sosa (1993 and ‘95) – in Cubs history to have a 30-30 showing. Crow-Armstrong also went 30-30 last year, and also became the only Cubs player to add 30 doubles to the mix. He did that again this season, too.
At the moment, Crow-Armstrong has 45 home runs, putting him alongside Sosa (five times), Ernie Banks (twice), Hack Wilson, Andre Dawson, Dave Kingman and Derrek Lee as the only Cubs to hit at least that many in a season. Crow-Armstrong is the first to do so since Lee had 46 in his 2005 campaign.
Crow-Armstrong also topped Billy Williams’ record (42 homers in 1970) for the most homers in a season in team history by a left-handed batter.
“It’s the best position-player season I’ve ever seen in my career,” Hoyer said. “He’s going to win the MVP. He’s going to win the Hank Aaron Award. He’s going to win the Platinum Glove. To me, that’s more impressive than any kind of triple crown that we would talk about.”
What has it been like to witness for Counsell?
“I’m kind of a fan. You’re part of it, right?” said the manager. “You’re just part of enjoying it. And I think it’s the things you remember about the job, moments like that and moments that he’s provided all of us.”

With the Chicago Cubs chasing their playoff spot for the 2026 season, Pete Crow-Armstrong was chasing a milestone of his own.
With just a few games to go, the Cubs' star center fielder punched his ticket.
He's officially a member of the 40-40 club.
PCA Makes History:
It was a good night for some history.
In a year when Crow-Armstrong is set to elevate from the face of the Cubs franchise to one of the faces of the entire league, he joined the 40-40 club on Thursday afternoon.
He swiped No. 39 in the third inning on Tuesday night. He got No. 40 on Thursday, and Crow-Armstrong has officially made history.
Crow-Armstrong has hit seven home runs and stolen seven bases on his way to the 40-40 Club. In August, Crow-Armstrong exploded with 14 home runs and 28 RBI in 28 games.
Earlier this month, he hit his 43rd home run of the season. That broke Billy Williams' Cubs record for left-handed hitters.
In September, it came down to stolen bases. The question was could Crow-Armstrong get to 40 steals by the end of the regular season?
He could. No. 39 and No. 40 came quickly this week. Crow-Armstrong made history.
By the numbers:
Crow-Armstrong joins an exclusive list of MLB players who achieved 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases in a season.
He joins Jose Canseco, Barry Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, Alfonso Soriano, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Shohei Ohtani as the seventh member of the 40-40 club.
Acuña is the only player to achieve a 40–70 season, stealing 70 bases in 2023. Ohtani is the only player to achieve a 50–50 season with 50 home runs and 50 stolen bases, which he accomplished in 2024.
What's next:
For the Cubs, the NL playoffs are next. The Wild Card round most likely awaits the Northsiders, who are on the verge of clinching a playoff berth.
For Crow-Armstrong, the individual awards will come later. After the 2026 MLB season and after a World Series winner is crowned, the league announces its MVP winners for the NL and AL.
It's not a given, but it feels like a foregone conclusion that Crow-Armstrong will unseat back-to-back winner Othani for the NL MVP honor.
This will punctuate a year that started back in March when Crow-Armstrong signed a six-year, $115 million extension through the 2032 season.
The regular season closes with Crow-Armstrong entering the 40-40 club. Soon, he might enter the MVP fraternity.

item.content:encoded:
Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base of the season on Thursday afternoon, a few weeks after belting his 40th career home run, which means the breakout star is now the seventh member of the 40-40 club in MLB history. He's all the way up to 45 home runs now to go with his 40 steals. Here's the historic 40th theft.
The previous entries:
| Player | Season | Home runs | Stolen bases |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jose Canseco | 1988 | 42 | 40 |
| Barry Bonds | 1996 | 42 | 40 |
| Alex Rodriguez | 1998 | 42 | 46 |
| Alfonso Soriano | 2006 | 46 | 41 |
| Ronald Acuña Jr. | 2023 | 41 | 73 |
| Shohei Ohtani | 2024 | 54 | 59 |
Canseco, Acuña and Ohtani won league MVP in those same seasons, and it appears PCA is headed in that direction.
As things stand, Crow-Armstrong is hitting .280/.374/.577 (157 OPS+) with 31 doubles, eight triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs and 40 steals. He leads the majors in runs, home runs, total bases and WAR (9.8) while leading the NL in slugging, OPS and OPS+. With the injury to Ohtani keeping him off the mound and later placing him on the IL, the path is clear for the first Cubs NL MVP since Kris Bryant took the honors in 2016. The hunch here is PCA wins the award unanimously.
But PCA isn't just having an MVP-caliber season; he's putting together one of the greatest individual seasons in franchise history. He's the first Cubs player to ever reach the 40-40 plateau, but before he came around, there had only been two 30-30 seasons, both by Sammy Sosa. PCA has now done it twice in a row and he's still only 24 years old.
Further, he's in rarified air in club history if we look at WAR, which takes hitting, baserunning and defense into account as a kind of "catch-all" stat (note: It is required by law here that I point out this isn't the only important stat and anyone who thinks otherwise is a fool).
Among Cubs position players, here are the top 10 seasons by Baseball Reference's WAR (heading into Tuesday):
1. Rogers Hornsby, 1929, 10.6 WAR
2. Sammy Sosa, 2001, 10.3
3. Ernie Banks, 1959, 10.2
t4. Pete Crow-Armstrong, 2026, 9.8
t4. Ron Santo, 1967, 9.8
6. Ernie Banks, 1958, 9.3
t7. Ron Santo, 1966, 8.9
t7. Ron Santo, 1964, 8.9
9. Ryne Sandberg, 1984, 8.5
10. Ernie Banks, 1955, 8.1
Over in the FanGraphs version, he scores even better. Here are the top 10 in Cubs history, where he has the best season in nearly a century:
1. Rogers Hornsby, 1929, 11.0
2. Pete Crow-Armstrong, 2026, 10.6
3. Sammy Sosa, 2001, 9.9
4. Ernie Banks, 1959, 9.7
5. Ron Santo, 1967, 9.5
6. Ernie Banks, 1958, 8.7
7. Ron Santo, 1964, 8.7
8. Ron Santo, 1966, 8.5
9. Hack Wilson, 1930, 8.0
10. Ryne Sandberg, 1984, 8.0
As a reminder, the WAR guidelines typically view 5.0 as an All-Star-caliber player and 8.0 as an MVP-caliber performer. Getting into double digits is generally considered an all-time great season.
The all-around performance here is what is staggering. The numbers at the plate say PCA has been one of the best hitters in baseball this season. He's in the top five in stolen bases and rates out excellently in other baserunning metrics. He's arguably the best defensive player in baseball, too, sitting in first in fielding run value and outs above average.
When you take a 40-40 player with a strong triple-slash line who is a terror on the bases and an incredible defensive player, you get one of the best individual seasons the Cubs franchise has ever seen.
And he's only 24 years old.
It's a special season for Pete Crow-Armstrong. As his Cubs eye the postseason, he'll look to lead them to a special season as a team next.

Across 182 innings (31 starts) in 2026, Seattle Mariners starting pitcher Logan Gilbert has recorded a 12-11 record with a 3.81 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 197 strikeouts. While Gilbert has still been a very useful pitcher for fantasy managers, he hasn't been quite as dominant this season as he has been in his peak years. After posting a 32.3% strikeout rate in 2025, Gilbert's strikeout rate has fallen to 26.7% in 2026. The 29-year-old's numbers have taken a considerable hit lately, as he's posted a 6.65 ERA across 21 2/3 innings in September. Surrendering the long ball has been a major issue for Gilbert in the second half of the season. Across 56 1/3 innings (10 starts) since the beginning of August, Gilbert has allowed 14 home runs (2.20 HR/9). Heading into his final scheduled start of 2026 against the Los Angeles Angels on Sunday, fantasy managers may want to temper expectations for the usually dependable Gilbert.--Will Brady

Across 653 plate appearances in 2026, San Diego Padres outfielder Jackson Merrill is hitting .252/.300/.459 with 26 home runs, 86 RBI, 82 runs scored, and 26 stolen bases. The 23-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, hitting .219 with 10 home runs across 396 plate appearances before the All-Star break. However, Merrill has been red hot in the second half, hitting .300 with 16 homers across his last 261 trips to the plate. Merrill has been particularly key to San Diego's late-season surge as an offense, hitting .325 with four home runs, 16 RBI, 10 runs scored, and two stolen bases over his first 85 plate appearances in September. The star center fielder has lowered his strikeout rate this month to 18.8% while also posting elite barrel (19.7%) and hard-hit (62.1%) rates. Heading into San Diego's final weekend of the regular season, Merrill profiles as one of the top five-category producers in all of fantasy baseball.--Will Brady

The 28-year-old got off to a rough start to the year, missing over two months with a shoulder injury and posting a 4.94 ERA across 27 1/3 innings in July. However, Brown has begun to rediscover his top form in recent outings. Across his last 33 1/3 innings (six starts), Brown is 3-0 with a 2.43 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, and 48 strikeouts. Brown has had issues with command all year long, and his 11.9% walk rate has led to an elevated WHIP. However, he's boosted his strikeout rate all the way up to 28.1% and has struck out 39.1% of the batters he's faced across his first four starts of September. Heading into his final start of the regular season on Saturday against the Athletics, Brown is beginning to look like the fantasy ace he was drafted to be ahead of 2026.--Will Brady

The 24-year-old's underlying batted-ball metrics are underwhelming, as he's logged just a 4.8% barrel rate and a 36.2% hard-hit rate. However, Bazzana's 11.2% walk rate is impressive for a young player and helps him get on base consistently and use his speed. Bazzana has also been red-hot of late, hitting .288 with six home runs, 15 RBI, and 11 runs scored across 69 plate appearances in September. If the former top prospect is starting to grow into his power, he could begin to emerge as one of the better second base options for fantasy managers. In leagues where he's on the waiver wire, Bazzana should be a priority target for fantasy managers.--Will Brady

Bell has kept his strikeout rate manageable at 19.9% while still posting solid barrel (9.5%) and hard-hit (42.0%) rates. Carlos Lagrange Could Join Yankees' Playoff Roster

Sep 24, 2026, 12:02 AM ET
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that right-handed pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange is "in the conversation" for a spot on the team's postseason roster for the wild-card series next week against the division-rival Boston Red Sox, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. The 23-year-old Dominican is the team's No. 3 prospect at MLB Pipeline, and he has been ramping up his throwing program since coming off the seven-day injured list on Sept. 16 with a sprained right shoulder. Lagrange went 1-4 this year at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, recording a 4.48 ERA, 1.35 WHIP, and 85:33 K:BB in 64 1/3 innings pitched across 19 appearances (11 starts). If Lagrange is pulled up to the Yankees' playoff roster, he would be making his major-league debut in the postseason in a relief role out of the bullpen. The 6-foot-7, 248-pounder has the tools to excel in high-leverage spots with an upper-90s fastball with armside run and multiple secondary pitches that can generate swings and misses consistently.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
Sep 23, 2026, 11:52 PM ET
Chicago Cubs right-hander Kevin Gausman (shoulder) came up wincing and in some apparent pain after diving to tag a runner out at third base during his start on Wednesday at Wrigley Field against the visiting Miami Marlins, according to Tony Andracki. Gausman was pulled from the game, but he was also at 101 pitches on the night. Manager Craig Counsell said that Gausman's left shoulder got extended awkwardly and "grabbed on him" on the play. He is now sore, and the Cubs will see how he feels in the next couple of days. Gausman is lined up to potentially start Game 1 or 2 next week in the wild-card series in the playoffs. The good news for the Cubs is that the injury is to the veteran's non-throwing arm as well. He came one out shy of a quality start for his fantasy managers on Wednesday, allowing two earned runs on six hits (one homer) while walking one and striking out seven in 5 2/3 frames for a no-decision. The 35-year-old veteran came into his final start of the regular season with a 9-12 record, 4.55 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 177 strikeouts in 172 innings pitched in 2026 with the Cubs and Toronto Blue Jays.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Tony Andracki
Sep 23, 2026, 10:59 PM ET
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that shortstop/second baseman Anthony Volpe could see some playing time at third base this week, per the Talkin' Yanks podcast. Volpe has mostly played shortstop in his MLB career, but he recently filled in at second base while Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. was sidelined by a thumb injury. With Chisholm Jr. back, it appears that New York could work Volpe into the mix at third base. The Yankees have gotten underwhelming production at the hot corner from Ryan McMahon, who has hit .210 with 11 home runs across 356 plate appearances in 2026. Volpe's numbers don't appear much better on the surface, as he's hit .244/.321/.335 with two home runs, 26 RBI, 24 runs scored, and 11 stolen bases across 234 plate appearances. However, the 25-year-old has been better in September, hitting .263 with four stolen bases across 40 trips to the plate this month.--Will Brady
Source: Talkin' Yanks
Chase Burns Working on Adding a Sinker


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:47 PM ET
Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Chase Burns (groin) was working on a sinker in his final starts before being placed on the 15-day injured list with a groin strain, per Charlie Goldsmith of the Charlie's Chalkboard Substack. Burns put together a dominant season in 2026, recording a 15-3 record with a 2.86 ERA, 1.17 WHIP, and 185 strikeouts across 154 1/3 innings (29 starts). However, Burns threw almost exclusively four-seam fastballs and sliders, mixing in the occasional changeup as well. Burns told Goldsmith that adding the sinker and continuing to develop his changeup should help him go deeper into games. If Burns can successfully add a sinker to his repertoire over the offseason, he could take his production to an even higher level in 2027.--Will Brady
Source: Charlie's Chalkboard - Charlie Goldsmith

Sep 23, 2026, 10:36 PM ET
Boston Red Sox left-hander Garrett Crochet (shoulder) will not appear in a regular-season game this week but is still in play to return during the postseason, per Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Crochet is currently on the 60-day injured list and has not pitched since late April due to shoulder and lat issues. However, he's been working toward a return and could be a factor out of the bullpen for Boston at some point in the playoffs. While 2026 has been a lost year for the 27-year-old, Crochet was one of the best pitchers in baseball in 2025. Across 205 1/3 innings (32 starts), he recorded an 18-5 record with a 2.59 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, and 255 strikeouts. Crochet also has experience as a reliever, making 54 appearances out of the bullpen for the Chicago White Sox in 2021.--Will Brady

Sep 23, 2026, 10:27 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies starting pitcher Jesus Luzardo (shoulder) played catch for a fourth straight day on Wednesday and is expected to progress to mound work "very soon," per Matt Gelb of The Athletic. Luzardo has been sidelined since early September by shoulder inflammation, but it appears he has a chance to work out of the bullpen for the Phillies in the National League Wild Card Series. Across 178 2/3 innings (29 starts) before the injury, the 28-year-old recorded a 14-5 record with a 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, and 221 strikeouts. Luzardo posted a career-best 30.4% strikeout rate and an elite 23.2% K-BB rate. While the talented left-hander is unlikely to be fully built up as a starter, getting Luzardo back in any capacity would still be a major boost for Philadelphia.--Will Brady
Source: The Athletic - Matt Gelb
Shane McClanahan Will Not Pitch in ALDS


Will Brady




Sep 23, 2026, 10:19 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash said that left-hander Shane McClanahan (forearm) is "not in play" for the team's American League Division Series roster, per Marc Topkin of the Tampa Bay Times. McClanahan has been sidelined since early September with left forearm tightness. While Cash did not rule McClanahan out if Tampa Bay advances past the ALDS, it appears the 29-year-old's return is not imminent. Injuries are nothing new for McClanahan, who missed all of 2024 and 2025 due to elbow and triceps issues. He was productive when healthy in 2026, recording a 10-7 record with a 3.36 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, and 106 strikeouts across 118 innings (24 starts). If McClanahan is able to return at some point in October, it seems likely that he would work out of the bullpen rather than attempting to build up as a starter.--Will Brady
Source: Tampa Bay Times - Marc Topkin
Sep 23, 2026, 10:10 PM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (calf) said he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the American League Wild-Card Series, per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. Judge is currently on the 10-day injured list as he battles a calf strain, but it appears he has a chance to be on the field when the Yankees open postseason play next Tuesday. It's been an injury-marred 2026 season for Judge, who was sidelined from late May until early September by a stress fracture in his rib and then immediately went back on the IL with the calf issue. He's also been below his incredibly lofty standard when healthy enough to play, hitting .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs scored, and five stolen bases across 285 plate appearances. Still, getting Judge back would obviously be a massive boost for a Yankees lineup that has largely struggled without its best player.--Will Brady

Boston Red Sox outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (hamstring) left Wednesday's game early against the Cleveland Guardians due to tightness in his right hamstring, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Before Rafaela was replaced in center field by Jarren Duran, he went 1-for-1 at the plate in his first game back from a stay on the 10-day injured list this month due to a right-quadriceps injury. “En el caso de Ronald, se podía ver de inmediato”, dijo el piloto de los Bravos, Walt Weiss. “Es un atleta fuera de serie, con un talento increíble. Entonces, es un poco diferente. Pero vaya, es muy divertido verlo cuando está encendido de esta manera”.
Lo único que ha frenado a Acuña en las últimas semanas fue la bola de foul que lo obligó a abandonar el juego de la noche del martes con una contusión en la espinilla izquierda. Afortunadamente, las radiografías y una tomografía computarizada no mostraron ninguna fractura. Por lo tanto, el dinámico jardinero podría perderse apenas un par de días.
Acuña llegó al juego de la noche del martes contra los Rojos con el segundo mejor OPS de las Mayores (1.119) desde el 28 de agosto, el día en que ajustó su postura. Su repunte ha aumentado el entusiasmo por lo que podría aportarles a los Bravos, campeones del Este de la Liga Nacional, durante la postemporada.
“Cuando está saludable y entra en una de estas rachas, es uno de los mejores jugadores del béisbol”, dijo el intermedista de los Bravos, Ozzie Albies. “No hay nada más que decir al respecto”.
Acuña estaba lejos de su mejor nivel cuando Weiss decidió dejar al veterano jardinero fuera de la alineación para un partido el 27 de agosto contra los Dodgers. El cinco veces convocado al Juego de Estrellas bateaba .228, con 13 jonrones y OPS de .732 en 81 encuentros de una temporada marcada por dos distensiones distintas en el tendón de la corva izquierdo.
Después de salir del estadio aquella noche, un frustrado Acuña le envió un mensaje de texto al coach de Grandes Ligas de los Bravos, el venezolano Eduardo Pérez, diciéndole que quería realizar prácticas de bateo temprano la tarde siguiente. Fue durante esa sesión que el veterano venezolano se alejó un par de pulgadas del plato, separó los pies unas cuantas pulgadas más y cerró su postura.
La combinación de esos cambios creó una postura muy similar a la que Acuña utilizó durante su temporada de JMV de la Liga Nacional en el 2023.
Acuña lució perdido durante los primeros meses de esta temporada. Además de intentar encontrar una postura cómoda y eficaz, buscaba ganar más confianza en sus dos rodillas operadas. Se rompió el ligamento cruzado anterior de la rodilla derecha en el 2021 y el de la izquierda en el 2024.
Desde el Día Inaugural hasta finales de abril, las dimensiones de la postura de Acuña fueron:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 31.3 pulgadas (distancia desde la parte frontal del plato hasta el centro de masa del bateador)
Distancia del plato: 25.3 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 31.6 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 34 grados abierta
Vimos la postura abierta durante los Entrenamientos Primaverales y en el Clásico Mundial de Béisbol. Pero su decisión de abrir el lado izquierdo y colocarse más atrás en la caja de bateo no produjo buenos resultados. Conectó dos cuadrangulares y registró OPS de .740 en los 34 juegos que disputó antes de sufrir una distensión en el tendón de la corva izquierdo el 2 de mayo.
Cuando Acuña regresó unas semanas después, cerró su postura (20 grados) y amplió ligeramente la distancia entre sus pies (33.5 pulgadas). Obtuvo algunos resultados alentadores, pero volvió a la lista de lesionados con otra distensión en el tendón de la corva el 10 de junio.
Cuando Acuña regresó nuevamente el 27 de julio, cerró aún más su postura y separó los pies una pulgada adicional.
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 30 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 25.3 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 34.4 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 14 grados abierta
Aun así, los resultados no aparecieron. Bateó .188, con seis vuelacercas y OPS de .614 en sus primeros 28 juegos tras regresar de la lista de lesionados. Fue entonces cuando Weiss decidió darle descanso a su superestrella para el último juego de la serie contra los Dodgers.
“Si te estoy dando un día libre, probablemente estés teniendo algunas dificultades”, destacó Weiss. “Así que también es un buen momento para tener un día de trabajo. Creo que lo aprovecharon bien”.
Así es como Acuña se ha colocado en la caja de bateo mientras exhibe un nivel digno de un JMV desde el 28 de agosto:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 29 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 27.4 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 36.4 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 12 grados
Esto se asemeja mucho más a la postura que utilizó durante su temporada del 2023. A lo largo de la campaña hubo intentos por hacer que volviera a esta postura, caracterizada por una base más amplia y una posición más cerrada. Pero Acuña tuvo dificultades para sentirse cómodo y, al mismo tiempo, mantener la confianza en la estabilidad de sus rodillas.
Postura del 2023:
Profundidad en la caja de bateo: 28.8 pulgadas
Distancia del plato: 27.9 pulgadas
Distancia entre los pies: 34.5 pulgadas
Ángulo de la postura: 12 grados abierta
Con esta postura más reciente, Acuña ha bateado .368, con siete bambinazos, uno cada 12.4 turnos al bate, y OPS de 1.107. Su tasa de batazos con el barril ha subido de 12.1% antes del 28 de agosto a 15.5%, mientras que su tasa de swings fallidos ha bajado de 30.1% a 26.5%.
Una gran diferencia ha sido el éxito de Acuña contra las rectas.
Antes del 28 de agosto
vs. recta de cuatro costuras: .119 de promedio (12 hits en 101 turnos), 32.4% de swings fallidos
vs. rectas de cuatro costuras de 95 mph o más: .119 de promedio (7 hits en 59 turnos), 31.8% de swings fallidos
Desde el 28 de agosto
vs. recta de cuatro costuras: .469 (15 hits en 32 turnos), 27.2% de swings fallidos
vs. rectas de cuatro costuras de 95 mph o más: .571 (8 hits en 14 turnos), 34.3% de swings en blanco
“Finalmente encontré mi timing”, dijo Acuña. “Simplemente me estoy divirtiendo ahí afuera”.

ATLANTA (AP) — Chris Sale struck out 10 and reached 200 Ks for the season, Mauricio Dubón delivered a winning RBI single in the 10th inning, and the Atlanta Braves defeated the Cincinnati Reds 3-2 on Wednesday night.
Matt Olson and Austin Riley hit solo homers for the Braves. Brent Suter (3-2) worked a scoreless 10th inning and earned the win.
Sale went 5 2/3 innings and was removed after recording his third strikeout of the game of Reds rookie Sal Stewart. The 37-year-old left-hander has reached 200 strikeouts nine times, which is the most of any pitcher since 2013. In his final start before the postseason, he allowed one run on four hits. Sale hit at least 99 mph on the radar gun on 12 of his 97 pitches.
Olson’s home run was his 41st of the season and tied the game at 1 in the sixth. Riley's homer tied the game at 2 in the seventh. Dubón was 2 for 4 with a walk and extended his hitting streak to 10 games.
Reds right fielder Juan Brito led off the game with a home run to center field off Sale. He went 2 for 4, including his third homer of the season.
Braves reliever Robert Suarez pitched for the first time since June 19 after being sidelined due to elbow inflammation. He pitched the seventh inning and gave up a leadoff triple to Matt McLain and a sacrifice fly to Will Banfield that gave the Reds a 2-1 lead. He threw 13 pitches.
Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. sat out after suffering a bone bruise when he fouled a ball off his shin in Tuesday's 4-0 loss to the Reds. Braves manager Walt Weiss said Acuña was asking to play and felt he could play right field Wednesday, but the Braves decided to be cautious with a postseason berth clinched.
Up next
Braves RHP Tyler Mahle (7-10, 3.81) will make his final start before the postseason against Reds RHP Brady Singer (6-15, 5.67) in the series finale Thursday.

The lineups are out for tonight's middle game between the Atlanta Braves and the Cincinnati Reds and the big news as far as Atlanta concerned was focused on injuries. There's good news to report on both fronts, as manager Walt Weiss is planning on Robert Suarez making his first big league appearance following his activation from a long stint on the IL and that Ronald Acuña Jr. is reportedly feeling fine after suffering a left shin contusion on Tuesday night. Acuña is out of the lineup tonight but he's no longer walking with a limp, so obviously some rest and (presumably) some ice did him well overnight.
In fact, it was to the point that Weiss reportedly stated during the pregame press conference that Acuña was apparently trying to convince the skipper to put him in the lineup for tonight's game. Obviously with an eye on the Postseason, that was never going to happen but it's nonetheless a good sign about how Acuña is feeling at the moment. Mark Bowman of MLB.com shared the report on social media.
Needless to say, the Atlanta Braves are going to need both Acuña and Suarez healthy and ready to go for October if they're going to have the best chance possible at making a deep Postseason run. Ever since Acuña reportedly widened his stance back on August 26, he's been hitting at a .348/.408/.641 clip with a .445 wOBA and 184 wRC+. Meanwhile, Suarez was carrying a 0.56 ERA and a 2.44 FIP across 32 innings pitched before he went on the IL following his appearance on June 19.
If both of those guys can keep up that pace upon their respective returns from injury then the Braves are going to be in a good spot heading into the Postseason. We'll see what happens going forward!

This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more.
Ronald Acuña Jr. of the Braves may be hitting .259 with career lows in exit velocity and hard-hit rate, but don’t be fooled by the overall stats. If the star outfielder can fight through a left shin contusion he suffered Tuesday night on a foul ball at the plate—he’s currently considered day-to-day—he’ll be a force to be reckoned with in October. Ever since mid-August when Acuña began to knock off the rust from two IL stints, he’s been a dangerous, dynamic hitter.
The tell-tale sign is how Acuña is getting to high fastballs he used to miss.
| Acuna vs. 95+ MPH | No. | BA | SLG | HR | Attack Angle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Through Aug. 22 | 315 | .183 | .268 | 1 | 9° |
| Since | 119 | .393 | .857 | 4 | 7° |
Pitchers were dominating Acuña with velocity over his hands. No more. Acuña has made the adjustment. While his barrel had been working underneath the pitch plane, now he is flattening his attack angle, as you can see here:
Acuña heads my list of hitters who are most likely to cap a disappointing year with a strong finish.
Down Year but Primed for Big October
1. Ronald Acuña Jr., Braves
2. Mookie Betts, Dodgers
3. Will Smith, Dodgers
4. Trevor Story, Red Sox
5. José Ramírez, Guardians
Gerrit Cole, Game 2 Starter?
Yankees righthander Gerrit Cole broke through a late-season slump with an improved outing Friday in Arizona (six innings, two earned runs).
As I said last week here, Cole has been throwing too many strikes in the middle of the plate. His fix: tighten the delivery to be more compact and move almost six inches on the rubber toward the third base side.
A frequent tinkerer, Cole began the season toward the center of the rubber but after the Red Sox pounded him for four runs June 27, he moved to the first base side July 3 and stayed there for 13 starts. But after his poor start Sept. 12 against the Mets, which included a career high of hard hits, he returned to the center.
Here you can see his foot position change on the rubber in his past two starts:
It’s the quickest fix to a command issue. You don’t need to change mechanics, just the lane in which the ball leaves your hand.
How did it work? His command was much better. Look at his fastball heat maps and it’s clear he did a better job of keeping the ball out of the center lane:
Cole Fastball Heat Maps
This start moved Cole closer to getting the ball ahead of Max Fried or Carlos Rodon (or both) in a wild-card series against Boston.
As usual, Cole pounded the zone. He has not issued a walk among 71 batters faced in his past three starts. But still a concern: the swing-and-miss still has not returned to his game. He had only six swings-and-misses against Arizona. His September whiff rate is 17%, down from 22.4% entering the month.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have a difficult decision in choosing who starts after Schlittler, a decision that should be based on how Cole, Fried and Rodon are throwing the ball rather than sheer numbers or opponent trends. The Red Sox are slightly better against left-handed pitching (24–15, .746 OPS) than right-handed (60–55, .713 OPS), though the return of Roman Anthony changes that a bit.

item.content:encoded:
In what will likely be his last regular season start for the Atlanta Braves this season, Chris Sale will be facing off against Andrew Abbott and the Cincinnati Reds.
Chris Sale is not the front runner for the Cy Young award, but will most certainly get some second and third place votes with his 2.18 ERA, 30.3 percent strikeout rate, and league leading strikeout to walk ratio of 6.13. Sale also leads the NL is best HR rate of 0.5 per nine innings, and best walk rate in the NL of 4.9 percent.
Side note, Chris Sale has the best career strikeout to walk ratio of all-time. Sale has also pitched 157.0 innings thus far this season, which is hurting his Cy Young chances to guys like Jacob Misiorowski. It could be argued that he has passed his fellow competitor Cristopher Sánchez, but Sánchez has a whopping 200.0 IP which is second in MLB behind Sandy Alcantara.
The Braves got a scare yesterday when Ronald Acuña fouled a ball off his shin, but luckily all the tests came back negative. The Braves have already clinched the division so a loss to the Reds yesterday was not a huge deal except the chances of a playoff bye are quickly fading. The offense looked bad again, so hopefully they can catch a spark again before the playoffs take off.
No Braves player has faced Abbott more than five at-bats. Ha-Seong Kim has a HR in his four at-bats and Ozzie Albies has a .600 average. Michael Harris has struggled to an OPS of .400 in his five at-bats, and Mauricio Dubón and Mike Yastrzemski are hitless in their three at-bats. Austin Riley is also hitless in five at-bats.
It is hard to make any type of prediction on such a limited history, but we can look at Abbott's numbers and see his 4.70 ERA is approximately eleven percent below average and his 1.472 WHIP is the worst of his four year career. This season he has struggled with walks giving up 4.2 per nine innings. The Braves need to be patient this even and take advantage of his weakness. It is no secret that the Braves struggle in the walk department. Their 7.7 percent is the third worst in MLB. To be fair, they strike out at a lower rate than the average team this season, but walks get runners on base to knock in.
The Reds are in the bottom six in RP ERA this season. The Braves have feasted on RPs all season long. The key to the game tonight seems to be be patient against Abbott because he gives up a lot of walks. Get to the bullpen, and strike. Chris Sale should keep the runs low to make this a pretty easy win on paper. The question is how many players will be resting today, especially with a high likelihood that Acuña will be letting his leg heal.

Ronald Acuña Jr. was unable to finish Tuesday's game against the Cincinnati Reds.
In the bottom of the third inning, the Atlanta Braves star fouled off a pitch that struck the inside of his left leg.
The outfielder looked like he was trying to walk it off, but he couldn't get past it and went down on the field. A trainer came out, and it looked like Acuña was in a lot of pain. He left the field, was pulled from the game, and was replaced by Brewer Hicklen.
Acuña missed time earlier this season due to a hamstring strain. He initially sustained the injury in May and then aggravated it again in early June. This caused him to miss more than a month and a half of action, and he didn't return until July 27.
The good news is that the Braves have already clinched both a postseason berth and the National League East title. The bad news is that if this injury is serious enough that Acuña needs to be added to the IL, any stint would affect his availability for Atlanta's first playoff series.
If Acuña is indeed sidelined for part of the Braves' playoff run, it would not be the first time he has missed out. The outfielder tore his right ACL in July 2021, months before the Braves went on to win the World Series over the Houston Astros.
The 28-year-old is the face of Atlanta's lineup, serving as the leadoff hitter. This season, he has played in 103 games and is slashing /.260/.352/.463 with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, and 20 stolen bases.
Acuña is three years removed from a dominant 2023 campaign where he tallied 41 home runs and 73 stolen bases for the first 40-70 season in MLB history.
The Braves have five more regular season games before the playoffs begin next week. If Acuña is sidelined, Atlanta will have to shuffle around its lineup, likely playing catchers Drake Baldwin and Sean Murphy in the same lineup with one as the DH. This would free up Mike Yastrzemski to take over in right field, but the Braves could also go with Hicklen or Dominic Smith as well.

item.content:encoded:
This is not the season Aaron Judge envisioned.
The three-time American League MVP is on the injured list with a calf strain, and the Yankees got a deflating update Tuesday. Judge is dealing with a “moderate” strain and has received a PPP injection to help speed healing. Manager Aaron Boone says the team is expecting him to miss the wild-card round of the playoffs.
That’s a massive blow for a team that has stumbled down the stretch a bit.
Judge missed 86 games earlier this season due to a rib injury. He finally returned to the lineup on Sept. 8 and, eight days later, left a game against the Twins after tweaking his calf during a swing. He went back on the IL on Sept. 18 and was eligible to come off as soon as Sunday. That is now unlikely, to say the least.
The 34-year-old has played in a full-season career-low 66 games this season and while pushing through the worst campaign of his career. Judge will end the regular season slashing .241/.360/.511, and his .871 OPS is the lowest he’s posted since a 27-game audition as a rookie in 2016. His wRC+ of 141 is his lowest since the COVID-shortened 2020 campaign.
He looked rusty when he came off the IL, and limped to a .513 OPS and a single home run in seven games.
It's been a lost season, but the Yankees have stayed afloat without him and entered Tuesday’s doubleheader with the Rays 89–66, with the top wild-card spot all but wrapped up. The team ranks 10th in runs scored and has leaned heavily on a pitching staff that boasts the best ERA in baseball at 3.22.
The Yankees are all but guaranteed to face the Red Sox in the opening round of the playoffs. Boston’s pitching staff ranks third in baseball with a 3.59 ERA, so runs figure to be at a premium in the series. The Red Sox won the season series, 7–6.
The list of Judge’s potential replacements in the lineup starts with Heliot Ramos, who has been manning right field, with Spencer Jones in center and Cody Bellinger in left. Ramos was added at the trade deadline and has struggled mightily to rack up hits in the Bronx. In 32 games with the team, he is slashing .172/.306/.366 with four home runs, 10 RBIs, 16 hits and a wRC+ of 91. He’s been bad, and he looks like the only option, as Trent Grisham appears far from returning. However, he has hit a home run in each of his last two games and is slashing .241/.305/.409 in September. That’s far from Judgian, but it’s at least some signs of life.
New York has gotten used to being without one of the best players on the planet for most of the season. The team deserves a lot of credit for getting this far, and can look to the 2021 Braves as inspiration in October—that Atlanta team lost Ronald Acuña Jr. for the season during the summer, entered the playoffs with just 88 wins and never faced elimination en route to a World Series title. And that Braves team didn’t have as talented of a pitching staff as these Yankees, who will also be granted a soft ALCS opponent with a worse record than them if they can advance that far.
With Judge down for the wild-card series, the Yankees will enter the playoffs on a down note no matter what happens over the season’s final week. But their biggest rival will still have to take down a plenty talented team in the hostile confines of Yankee Stadium—perhaps right after completing its season a day earlier. The injury gods may not be on the Yankees’ side right now, but if there’s one team the baseball gods have smiled upon throughout the sport’s existence, it’s them. Don’t count New York out yet.

Ronald Acuña Jr. suma su tercera temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas en MLB y entra al top 3 entre venezolanos.
Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue escribiendo su nombre en la historia del béisbol venezolano. El outfielder de los Bravos de Atlanta cerró otra temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas, un logro que pocos han repetido con tanta consistencia. Acuña alcanza su tercera campaña 20-20 y con eso se suma a un grupo selecto de compatriotas que marcaron época en Grandes Ligas.
El camino no fue sencillo. Las lesiones interrumpieron su ritmo en varios momentos y limitaron su presencia en la alineación. Aun así, el criollo encontró la forma de producir cuando estuvo disponible y dejó números que respaldan su calidad. Su combinación de poder y velocidad lo mantiene como una pieza clave en el ataque de Atlanta y como referencia obligada al hablar de los mejores peloteros de Venezuela.
Este hito llega en un año en el que muchos dudaban de su capacidad para mantener el nivel de años anteriores y en el que las lesiones volvieron a estar presentes. Pese a esto los números de Acuña confirman su recuperación, algo que resulta clave tomando en cuenta que nos acercamos a octubre y que Atlanta lo necesita sano para poder pelear en playoffs.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr.: velocidad, poder y una nueva página en MLB
Qué significa la temporada 20-20 de Ronald Acuña Jr. en 2026
Una campaña 20-20 exige un buen desempeño en dos facetas claves de la ofensiva: pegarle fuerte a la bola y saber correr las bases con inteligencia. Acuña cumplió con ese doble requisito en 2026 y con eso llegó a su tercera temporada 20-20 en la MLB. Sus otras dos veces con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas llegaron en 2019 y 2023, años en los que también dejó un perfil ofensivo completo, con poder en el bate y presión en las bases.
Acuña acumula 103 partidos en 2026, con 454 apariciones en el plato, 102 hits, 55 carreras impulsadas y 60 anotadas. Esos números reflejan un rendimiento sólido para un jugador que pasó por dos distensiones en el corva izquierda y que en varios tramos de la temporada no estuvo al 100%. Aun con esos obstáculos, el criollo fue capaz de dejar muy buenos números en esta temporada regular.
Este tipo de registro no depende solo de fuerza. También exige una excelente lectura de lanzamientos, disciplina en el plato y timing para robar algo que lo ha caracterizado a lo largo de su carrera. Hay que recordar que Acuña suma 225 bases robadas de por vida y 206 jonrones en su carrera regular, cifras que lo ubican en un nivel distinto dentro de la ofensiva venezolana en la MLB.
El club selecto de venezolanos con temporadas 20-20 en MLB
Pocos peloteros de Venezuela han logrado una campaña 20-20. El grupo lo encabezan Bobby Abreu, Carlos González y José Altuve, tres nombres que definieron épocas distintas y que dejaron huella en sus respectivas franquicias. Acuña se une a ese trío y con su tercera vez se ubica en el top 3 histórico de jonroneros venezolanos en Grandes Ligas, un escalón que pocos alcanzan y que mide impacto real en el juego.
Bobby Abreu marcó el estándar con la marca 20-20 en 9 temporadas a lo largo de su carrera en MLB, un número que refleja su combinación de poder y velocidad durante más de una década. Carlos González alcanzó ese registro en 4 ocasiones durante sus 12 campañas en la liga mayor, con picos de producción que lo llevaron a la élite del bateo. José Altuve, por su parte, suma 3 temporadas 20-20 con los Astros de Houston, un logro que respalda su perfil de bateador de contacto con velocidad en las bases.
La marca de Acuña también tiene un componente de resistencia. Llegar tres veces a 20-20 implica mantener salud relativa y rendimiento en distintos momentos de la carrera. El criollo ya tiene un MVP en 2023, un Rookie del Año en 2018 y un récord histórico de 40-70 en esa misma campaña del MVP. Esos logros, sumados a su tercera temporada 20-20, lo convierten en referencia para la nueva generación de peloteros venezolanos.

Por qué Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue siendo clave para los Bravos y para Venezuela
Atlanta construye su ataque alrededor de la versatilidad. Acuña ofrece poder desde la parte alta del orden al bate, capacidad para estirar hits y presión constante sobre la defensa rival. Esa combinación hace que su presencia en el lineup, incluso con minutos limitados debido a las lesiones, cambie la dinámica del juego.
Acuña apenas tiene 28 años y ya suma tres campañas 20-20, una cifra que deja espacio para seguir creciendo. Su historial de poder y velocidad, sumado a su capacidad de ajuste, lo pone en ruta para añadir más temporadas con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas. La gran incógnita ahora es si podrá igualar o superar las 9 veces de Bobby Abreu, el récord entre venezolanos en MLB. El tiempo dirá si el criollo se acerca a esa marca o si incluso la deja atrás.

The Chicago White Sox lost 121 games just two seasons ago.
Now, they are fighting to make the postseason and win the division for the first time since 2021.
Chicago is one game behind the Cleveland Guardians for first place in the AL Central standings.
To book an automatic trip to the ALDS, the White Sox will need productive weeks from the everyday players.
However, it may also include their bench players, some of whom are having a better offensive year than others.
Outfielder and shortstop Luisangel Acuna, the younger brother of Atlanta Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr., is having a poor season at the plate.
In fact, Acuna's offensive performance has been one of the worst in the Majors. Bleacher Report's Zachary D. Rymer named him Chicago's worst player of 2026.
"To be fair, Edgar Quero has taken exactly as many plate appearances (217) as Acuña and has been even more of a straggler, to the tune of -0.8 rWAR. At least he's off the roster, whereas Acuña is still doing the bad kind of damage," Rymer wrote.
In 98 games, Acuna has a .227/.260/.261 slash line with just one home run and a .522 OPS.
"He has only a 47 OPS+ for the season, making him 53 percent worse than the average hitter. Among hitters with at least 200 plate appearances, only three have been less productive at the plate," Rymer added.
Acuna may not see much playing time in the postseason, but he can provide value with his legs.
The 24-year-old has 17 stolen bases in 23 attempts and ranks in the 98th percentile for sprint speed.

item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

We’ve made it to the final week of the regular season. There are still two divisions in the American League up for grabs, a couple of long-shot playoff hopefuls looking to make a last-minute run, and playoff seeding to fight over. It should make for a dramatic end to a great season.
Our power rankings use a modified Elo rating system. If you’re familiar with chess rankings, you’ll know that Elo is an elegant ranking format that measures teams’ relative strength and is very reactive to recent performance. To avoid overweighting recent results during the season, we weigh each team’s raw Elo rank using our coin flip playoff odds (specifically, we regress the playoff odds by 50% and weigh those against the raw Elo ranking, increasing in weight as the season progresses to a maximum of 25%). The weighted Elo ranks are then displayed as “Power Score” in the tables below. As the best and worst teams sort themselves out between now and October, they’ll filter to the top and bottom of the rankings, while the exercise remains reactive to hot streaks and cold snaps. If you’re looking for a visual representation of the ups and downs of your team throughout the season, look no further than the brand new Power Rankings Board in the FanGraphs Lab.
First up are the full rankings, presented in a sortable table. Below that, I’ve grouped the teams into tiers with comments on a handful of clubs. You’ll notice that the official ordinal rankings don’t always match the tiers — there are times where I take editorial liberties when grouping teams together — but generally, the ordering is consistent. One thing to note: The playoff odds listed in the tables below are our standard Depth Charts odds, not the coin flip odds that are used in the ranking formula.

It was a great week for the Brewers. They won their fourth straight NL Central title and sixth in the last nine years, and also set another franchise record for wins in a single season, one year after setting the previous record. They now have a chance to win 100 games for the first time in club history this week and still have the top seed in the NL to play for.
The Rays swept the Athletics and won their series against the Red Sox last week to put some distance between themselves and the Yankees in the AL East race. The gap in the division is now six games, and even though the two rivals play each other four times during the final week of the season, it would take a massive collapse from Tampa Bay to upset the current standings. Because the Rays also currently lead the season series with the Yankees, 6-3, all they need is to win one of the four games in New York to take the division title. With Shane McClanahan still recovering from his forearm injury — his availability for the playoffs is up in the air — Freddy Peralta has stepped up to lead the pitching staff over the last few weeks. Across his last five starts, he’s allowed just three runs in 28 2/3 innings. That’s the kind of production the Rays were hoping to get when they acquired him at the trade deadline.

The Dodgers are getting all their pieces in place for the postseason. Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki will be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and Shohei Ohtani should follow on Wednesday. There’s a lingering question about Blake Snell’s status after he injured his groin last week, but it sounds like he’ll be able to make a start during the final weekend of the season. And even though the majority of the year has been a slog for Kyle Tucker, his bat seems to have finally woken up at the right time; he collected nine hits and three home runs last week.
Having won 13 of their last 14 games, the Padres are peaking at exactly the right moment. They’ve surged five games ahead of the Diamondbacks and one ahead of the Phillies in the NL Wild Card standings, and are now tied with the Cubs for the top spot. San Diego’s final series of the season against Arizona still looms large, especially if the Friars stumble against the Dodgers in the series beforehand. You’re probably familiar with Fernando Tatis Jr.’s hot streak — he blasted four home runs last week to bring his total in September up to eight — but the biggest contributor to the Padres’ success recently has been Ty France. He had 12 hits and a home run last week and has posted a fantastic 168 wRC+ during the second half of the season.
After a couple of years away from the top, the Braves are NL East champions again — it’s their seventh division title in the last nine years. Atlanta’s dominance this year has been a welcome return to form. Even though his season has been a bit up and down, Ronald Acuña Jr. is looking like the superstar that won the MVP back in 2023 again. Last week, he smacked three home runs, including a go-ahead grand slam on Saturday, and is running a 191 wRC+ in September.
A little more than a week after being activated off the IL, Aaron Judge is back on the shelf, this time with a calf injury sustained on Wednesday. His availability for the playoffs is still up in the air, though he’s confident that he’ll be able to return sooner rather than later. Thankfully, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and there’s some confidence that Trent Grisham will also be ready to return for the postseason. It helps that Ben Rice has bounced back from a rough August to post a 192 wRC+ in September. Still, Judge’s injury is a major blow to the Yankees’ hopes for a deep October run.

Even though the Red Sox lost both of their series last week, they managed to clinch a postseason berth on Sunday. It’s the cap to a remarkable turnaround after the team looked completely lost in mid-June. Boston can officially secure the second Wild Card spot with a couple of wins against the Guardians this week. Then the team can turn its attention to the Yankees and the rematch of last year’s Wild Card matchup between these two historic rivals.
Nothing is going to come easy for the Phillies over the next few weeks. The team placed Jesús Luzardo on the IL last week with a shoulder injury, but thankfully, it sounds like he’ll be ready to pitch in the playoffs. But before they count their chickens, they need to actually clinch a playoff spot. Philadelphia is four games up on the Diamondbacks in the NL Wild Card race, but its upcoming opponents are no cake walk; the Phillies have the Brewers and Rays on the schedule to finish off the regular season. Facing two of the best teams in baseball is quite a test ahead of the postseason, and the Phillies haven’t exactly been playing well lately.
The biggest concern for the Cubs right now is the status of Alex Bregman. He was struck by a foul ball in the face while standing in the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game and was taken to the hospital for further evaluation. Alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bregman has been one of the best hitters in baseball since the All-Star break. It would be a huge blow if the third baseman had to miss any significant amount of time at this point in the season. As for Crow-Armstrong, he’s two stolen bases away from joining the 40/40 club. He put a few finishing touches on his MVP case last week by bopping four more home runs, bringing his season total up to 45.

There was some upheaval in the two division races represented in this tier. Entering last week one game behind the White Sox in the AL Central standings, the Guardians took two of three games against the South Siders in a dramatic series, which included a walk-off on Tuesday and an improbable go-ahead homer on Wednesday. From there, although Chicago took advantage of playing — and winning — on Thursday while Cleveland was off to pull back into a tie atop the division, the Guardians just kept winning, sweeping the the Athletics over the weekend to bring their winning streak to five. José Ramírez finally broke out of his extended slump, tallying nine hits, a home run, and four stolen bases last week.
As for the White Sox, they won three of their four games against the the Tigers, but that one loss was enough to drop them to a game behind Cleveland in the Central. Still, the Sox have a three-game cushion for the final AL Wild Card spot, and they own the tiebreaker over the Guardians, meaning both first place and a potential first-round bye are still in their sights. Miguel Vargas is carrying most of the load for the lineup right now, hitting three home runs last week, but he needs some support if Chicago wants to make some noise in the postseason.
Over in the AL West, the Astros were swept by the Braves this past weekend, allowing the Rangers to jump into first place with a .500 record. Texas enters this week one game up, but crucially Houston holds the tiebreaker. If the Rangers can manage to hang on, it would be just their second postseason appearance in the last decade. The last time they made the playoffs, they won the World Series.
The Houston bullpen was responsible for the backbreaking losses on Saturday and Sunday, but the lack of offense has been a much bigger problem. Over the Astros’ last 10 games, they’ve scored more than four runs in a game just once. Yordan Alvarez looked fine last week (eight hits, including two home runs) after his ankle scare the previous weekend, and Jeremy Peña has been great too (10 hits, three homers), but the rest of the lineup has been struggling. They’re three games back and have the Astros to contend with if they want to try and sneak into that final Wild Card spot. The series between the Orioles and Mets last week in Queens turned out to be more interesting than you’d expect from two teams mired in hugely disappointing seasons. Pete Alonso made his first appearance as a member of the opposing team at Citi Field and wound up hitting his 300th career home run on Tuesday, a game-tying shot in the ninth inning. He received a huge ovation from the hometown crowd, which drew some irksome comments from a few Mets players and staff after the game. Baltimore wound up sweeping New York to cut its deficit in the AL Wild Card race to 2.5 games. Alas, a sweep by the Brewers over the weekend slammed the door shut on any playoff hopes the O’s still had.
Even though the Marlins’ season essentially ended with that 12-game losing streak back in July, they have made some significant progress in their quest to become a contending club. Otto Lopez looks like a star they can build the lineup around, while Eury Pérez and Max Meyer should be strong enough to anchor the pitching staff in the years ahead. There’s also a cohort of young prospects in the upper minors who should be making their debuts soon. The future in Miami is brighter than it’s been in a while.

Sal Stewart has been excellent as De La Cruz’s sidekick, but the starting rotation has struggled mightily, and the big injury to Hunter Greene has thrown the ceiling of that group up in the air heading into next year. It took a lot longer than expected, but the Twins were finally eliminated from the playoff race last week. It was a drama-filled week, too. They won a wild extra-inning walk-off affair against the Yankees on Wednesday and then were walked-off twice against the Angels between two shutout victories over the weekend.
